prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, through the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments

statement.case_for: The Higgs boson is the clearest clue from nature that fundamental physics has produced in my working life. Two independent experiments found the same particle in 2012, and a decade of Run 2 and Run 3 coupling measurements has since turned a discovery into a precision programme that anchors every discussion of naturalness and what lies beyond the Standard Model. The 2013 prize honoured the theory; the experimental half remains unrecognised, and that gap grows less defensible each year. In the spirit of putting the discovery first and the people second, I find no other shortlisted item where the scientific result is so unambiguous, so permanent and so central to our picture of how the universe is built. I have moved my proposed trio from my opening ballot to Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee. Three colleagues (Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce) independently landed on names within this set. Jenni and Virdee are the founding spokespersons and conceptual drivers of ATLAS and CMS, and Gianotti led ATLAS at the moment of announcement, so the trio spans both experiments, the founding and the delivery.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and I do not think it can be argued away. A discovery made by two collaborations of thousands is being assigned to three leaders, and every trio drops one of four credited people (Della Negra, whom I named in my opening and who has an equally strong CMS founding claim, is now left out). Pearce and Lindroth both noted that the statutes favour individuals, and that tension is not resolved by calling the leaders representative. A committee could reasonably conclude that the cleanest, most defensible prize on this shortlist is the optical lattice clock, where two names match two identifiable inventive steps, and that the Higgs is too diffuse to credit fairly. The 2013 prize could also be read as having already recognised the discovery. I take that objection seriously, and I would rather lose this argument on attribution grounds than win it by pretending the attribution is easy.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first: Katori's magic-wavelength idea plus Ye's record performance give a clean two-person prize, with direct atomic-structure insight into why the systematics are controlled, and she defers to particle colleagues on the Higgs.
responses.response: I accept that B008 has the best attribution on the shortlist, and your point about direct knowledge of the systematic shifts carries weight with me. Where I differ is on the kind of achievement. The clock is a superb invention that lets us measure what we could not before, but it extends a tradition the committee honoured in 2005 and 2012, while the Higgs is a discovery of a new particle that settled a half-century question. I would not call the clock a poor choice, and it is my first alternative, but I do not think clean attribution should by itself outweigh the size of the result.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven opening of a new window, with Halzen and Karle as a compact pair, and he rates the Higgs only fifth because of the three-of-four problem and the argument that 2013 already covered the discovery.
responses.response: I agree with you that IceCube is a real discovery and that Halzen and Karle are a natural compact pair; it was fourth on my own ballot. My reservation is the one you list yourself: most of the diffuse flux has no identified source, and TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are at moderate significance. I would call it very promising rather than finished. On the Higgs I disagree that 2013 settles it. That prize recognised the prediction; the observation was a separate achievement. I do, however, share your concern about the allocation, and I have adopted the Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee trio you proposed, since I cannot defend my earlier choice over yours on the record.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a mature, clean and lasting enabling advance, and puts the Higgs second while admitting that dropping one of four founders is a judgement rather than a result of the record.
responses.response: I agree entirely that the choice among the four is a judgement and not something the record settles. On B009 I would press the question you raise yourself about whether this is physics. The result is certainly mature and the Rose-Haider-Urban chain is clean, but the committee's own custom favours discoveries about nature, and a corrector is a tool for seeing, mostly used in materials science and chemistry. I would take it seriously as an alternative only if colleagues are convinced that it belongs in physics.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a new state of matter with a theory-experiment-spectroscopy story, and treats B035 (twisted bilayer graphene) as a strong second.
responses.response: The conceptual weight of topological band theory is not in doubt, and I would be glad to hear more about the field from you. My difficulty is attribution: Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson all point out that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect and are outside the supplied credit, and that the 3D work is a separate story. A prize that leaves out a pivotal step is exactly the type I would worry about later. As for twisted bilayer graphene, I ranked it sixth because the pairing mechanism is unresolved, which I find hard to square with the maturity we usually require.

uncertainties: Which three of the four credited ATLAS and CMS leaders best represent the decisive contributions is a judgement I cannot settle from the supplied material, and I have not independently verified the leadership histories.
Whether the committee is willing to honour a collaboration-scale discovery through individuals, and whether the Higgs would then set a precedent that is hard to apply later.
Whether the clean attribution of the optical lattice clock should outweigh the larger significance of the Higgs in the final ballot.
How far the IceCube source associations and the twisted bilayer graphene pairing mechanism will mature, which affects whether they are timely this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My supervisor David Gross is not connected to any shortlisted candidate, and my work in string theory and cosmology is remote from every shortlisted field.
